introduction: These readings sort love into its kinds and trace its paths. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá names four: the love of God for his creation, of the creature for God, of God for his own beauty, and of people for one another, which is real only when it springs from the others; Bahá’u’lláh counts the journeys of the lover; later passages say that we cannot love everyone personally but can love all for God's sake, that love is shown in deeds, and that it is the foundation of religion and the force that transforms. The guide itself quotes the Gospels and the letters of John. All fifty-nine quotations are read here beside fifty-nine from elsewhere. Most stand alongside: the Song of Songs, Plato's ladder of love, Rumi's reed and Saadi's moth, Augustine, Dante, Paul's hymn to charity, Confucius, Hillel, the Dhammapada. Seven push back or add a side: Dostoevsky's lover of humanity who cannot love a person, Mencius defending the special love of family, Montaigne's 'because it was he', Tennyson's nature red in tooth and claw, Machiavelli on fear and love, Spinoza on the love with which God loves himself, and Shakespeare's unaltering love.
questions: Which of the four kinds of love do you understand least? What would it be to know it better?
'Love the creatures for the sake of God and not for themselves.' Montaigne loved his friend 'because it was he'. What does each kind of love see that the other misses?
We are told we cannot love everyone personally but must love all humanity. Dostoevsky's character found the two pulling apart. How are they kept together?
Mencius thought love without distinction denies what we owe our parents. Do the readings set family love aside, or build on it?
'If I love you, I need not continually speak of my love.' How is love known?
Machiavelli thought fear the safer bond. Where have you seen love actually change something?

outside.why: John's Gospel begins the first kind of love here: God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son.
Jeremiah hears God say: I have loved thee with an everlasting love; with lovingkindness have I drawn thee.
A psalm voices the love that goes the other way: as the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee.
Augustine found three things wherever there is love: he that loves, that which is loved, and love.
Leviticus commands the fourth kind: thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.
This is the bush of Exodus, which burned with fire and was not consumed.
Dante's poem ends with the Love which moves the sun and the other stars.
Paul tells his friends that he thanks God upon every remembrance of them.
Jesus gave a new commandment: that ye love one another, as I have loved you.
Plato's Diotima describes love climbing by degrees, from beautiful things to a beauty wondrous in its nature.
Spinoza held that the mind's intellectual love of God is the very love with which God loves himself. Is that the love 'from God to God' the reading names first?
Julian of Norwich asked what her Lord meant, and was answered: love was his meaning.
Hosea has God say: I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love.
The Song of Songs says in seven words what the lover knows: my beloved is mine, and I am his.
The same Song tells of seeking by night him whom the soul loveth, and not finding him.
And of being found: he brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love.
Rumi's reed-flute laments its separation from the reed-bed, and its notes move men and women to tears.
Saadi tells the bird of the morning to learn love from the moth, which burnt, lost its life, and found no voice.
Plato's Socrates calls the madness of love the greatest of heaven's blessings.
Thomas à Kempis wrote that love is a great thing, which by itself makes everything that is heavy, light.
Augustine says to God: you have made us for yourself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in you.
Rabia asked for neither this world nor the next: thou art enough for me.
A psalmist says: one thing have I desired of the Lord, to behold the beauty of the Lord.
Proverbs says that a friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
Jesus said: greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
The Song of Songs says that if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned.
A character in Dostoevsky confesses: the more I love humanity in general, the less I love man in particular. Is a love for all that is not personal a love at all?
Jesus answered 'who is my neighbour?' with a stranger who stopped on the road for a wounded man.
Jesus asked: if ye love them which love you, and salute your brethren only, what do ye more than others?
Confucius, asked by a disciple what benevolence is, answered in four words: it is to love all men.
Mencius objected that to love all equally is not to acknowledge the special claim of a father. Are the 'imperfect bonds' of family obstacles to love, or its school?
Montaigne could give no reason for loving his friend but this: because it was he, because it was I. What is lost if people are loved for God's sake and not for themselves?
Paul asks that in lowliness of mind each esteem other better than themselves.
Paul tells the Galatians how their liberty should be used: by love serve one another.
John's first letter says: let us not love in word, neither in tongue, but in deed and in truth.
Paul says that speech without love is as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.
John's first letter repeats the message heard from the beginning: that we should love one another.
Paul lists what love includes: it suffers long and is kind, envies not, is not easily provoked, thinks no evil.
Paul tells the Colossians: above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness.
Spinoza reasoned that hatred is increased by being reciprocated, and can be destroyed by love.
Paul ranks them: faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.
Shelley saw the same law in nature: nothing in the world is single; all things by a law divine in one spirit meet and mingle.
Tennyson set the trust that love is creation's final law against nature, red in tooth and claw. Is attraction the whole story of the natural world?
Saadi wrote that the sons of Adam are limbs of each other, created of one essence.
Shakespeare says that love is not love which alters when it alteration finds. Is a constant human love material, or already spiritual?
Paul is persuaded that neither death nor life can separate us from the love of God.
Genesis says: let us make man in our image, after our likeness.
John's first letter says that he that loveth not knoweth not God, for God is love.
Aristotle said that the first cause produces motion as being loved, and all other things move by being moved.
Blake wrote that we are put on earth a little space, that we may learn to bear the beams of love.
Jesus points to a Father who makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good.
Donne wrote that no man is an island; any man's death diminishes me, because I am involved in mankind.
Whitman said that whoever walks a furlong without sympathy walks to his own funeral drest in his shroud.
Hillel summed up the Torah: that which is hateful to you do not do to another; the rest is interpretation.
The Dhammapada says that hatred does not cease by hatred at any time; hatred ceases by love.
A psalm says: behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.
Ephesians prays that its readers be rooted and grounded in love, and know the love which passeth knowledge.
Isaiah has God say: can a woman forget her child? yet will I not forget thee.
Machiavelli advised princes that it is much safer to be feared than loved. Is love a power that changes the world, or only those already willing?
